title: When Shared Knowledge Hurts: Spectral Over-Accumulation in Model Merging
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Summing task updates repeatedly counts the knowledge they share, inflating top singular values and suppressing task-specific components elsewhere.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; task matrices feed a bar chart via a big arrow
description: The left panel shows three colored weight-update grids (ΔW1 yellow, ΔW2 blue, ΔW3 red). Curved gray connectors link each grid to a green ellipse labeled 'Shared Knowledge'. Three more connectors run from the ellipse to icons for Task A, B and C, which are a browser window, a robot and a rising chart. A large yellow arrow labeled 'Excessive Accumulation' points right to a schematic bar chart whose y-axis is 'Singular Value'. The 'Top Subspace' bar is a tall yellow task-specific block topped by hatched blue and red segments. A brace marks those two segments as 'Shared Knowledge'. The 'Bottom Subspace' bar is a short yellow block. A legend at bottom right says 'Task-Specific Expert Knowledge'. The eye goes first to the stacked hatched bar and the green ellipse.
caption: Shared knowledge accumulation in model merging. When merging task matrices (∆Wi) from multiple tasks, shared knowledge that aligns across tasks can be over-counted, resulting in singular-value inflation in the merged model’s spectrum. This inflation is concentrated in a few top spectral subspaces, causing the merged model to be dominated by shared directions, while taskspecific components in the remaining subspaces are suppressed.
abstract: Model merging combines multiple fine-tuned models into a single model by adding their weight updates, providing a lightweight alternative to retraining. Existing methods primarily target resolving conflicts between task updates, leaving the failure mode of over-counting shared knowledge unaddressed. We show that when tasks share aligned spectral directions (i.e., overlapping singular vectors), a simple linear combination repeatedly accumulates these directions, inflating the singular values and biasing the merged model toward shared subspaces. To mitigate this issue, we propose Singular Value Calibration (SVC), a training-free and data-free post-processing method that quantifies subspace overlap and rescales inflated singular values to restore a balanced spectrum. Across vision and language benchmarks, SVC consistently improves strong merging baselines and achieves state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, by modifying only the singular values, SVC improves the performance of Task Arithmetic by 13.0%. Code is available at https://github.com/lyymuwu/SVC.
